deep.reconstruction:
Setting (cote 154, 1983-84). Grothendieck is building a combinatorial model for the deformation theory of a system Σ of pseudo-lines in the projective plane. Γ(Σ) is an oriented graph. Its vertices D are combinatorial configurations. Its oriented edges are specializations D → D', in which a small triangle T of the arrangement collapses to a triple point. There are also 'pseudo-specializations' and 'neutral' edges. Around each vertex D he places a cyclically ordered 'polygon' Pol(D). Its vertices are the edges of Γ(Σ) at D: specialization edges leaving D, generalization edges arriving at D, and neutral edges. The polygon carries weights or gradations on its arcs, with additivity relations (previous page: poids(α')+poids(β')+poids(ω)=poids(γ)). It also carries an antipodal involution.

On this page:
(1) The figures show orange pseudo-lines crossing a green line, with marked intervals between crossing points. An interval may correspond to a vertex of Σ that gives a 'free edge' of Γ, one with an origin but no endpoint.
(2) He proposes to complete Pol(D) into a larger polygon Pol*(D). He adds the antipodes of all specialization and pseudo-specialization vertices as free boundary edges. The antipode of a true specialization is again a specialization, not a pseudo-specialization; the next page confirms this.
(3) Key claim: a specialization D → D' induces an isomorphism of Pol*(D) onto a sub-polygon of Pol*(D'), but not onto all of it. Collapsing T can create new triangles, hence new (pseudo-)specialization vertices. This happens when one of the faces adjacent to T, or one of its lateral faces, is a quadrilateral, which becomes a triangle after the collapse. The central figure shows triangles t, t' next to T with a dashed green curve.
(4) The NBs say:
- the weight of an arc of Pol*(D) may be zero (linked to generalization);
- the antipody of Pol*(D) is intrinsic;
- the weights are stable under antipody.
Compatibility of Pol*(D) → Pol*(D') with the weights is stated as equality of the weights of corresponding arcs.
(5) When the map is not an isomorphism, adjacent vertices (D',a), (D',a') of Pol*(D') are missing from the image. The next page then requires the gradation of an arc of Pol*(D) to equal the sum of the gradations of the sub-arcs in Pol*(D'). He also asks for a theory of 'gradation on a sub-polygon of a graded polygon'.

Overall aim: axiomatize the local structure of the specialization graph of pseudo-line arrangements (cyclic order, orientation, antipody, gradation). The question raised on the next page is whether the restriction maps follow from the other structures.
errors: No outright error. The claim that collapsing a triangle turns an adjacent quadrilateral into a triangle, creating new flippable triangles, is the standard combinatorics of triangle flips. The exact meaning of 'faces latérales' versus 'faces adjacentes' is ambiguous on the page.

The setup is exploratory: Pol*(D), 'pseudo-spécialisation' and the weight relations are never defined precisely here. Whether the antipody is well defined on Pol*(D) is asserted ('intrinsèque'), not proved.

ideas.what: Graph Γ(Σ) of combinatorial pseudo-line configurations, with oriented edges given by specialization (collapse of a triangle to a triple point).
ideas.modern_name: Flip graph / stratification of the space of pseudo-line arrangements (triangle flips, Reidemeister-III moves, oriented-matroid realization strata)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956) for flip connectivity; Goodman–Pollack, Björner–Las Vergnas–Sturmfels–White–Ziegler (Oriented Matroids, 1993); Mnëv (1988) for strata
ideas.where_published: Possibly alluded to in Esquisse d'un programme (1984) among tame-topology themes; unsure

ideas.what: Local link polygon Pol(D)/Pol*(D) at a configuration: cyclically ordered incident edges typed as specialization, generalization or neutral, with antipodal involution and arc gradations.
ideas.modern_name: Link of a stratum in a stratified space / ribbon-graph structure, with graded edge weights
ideas.usually_credited_to: No specific attribution for this exact structure

ideas.what: A specialization D→D' induces an embedding of Pol*(D) as a sub-polygon of Pol*(D'), not an isomorphism, because quadrilaterals adjacent to T become new triangles.
ideas.modern_name: Change of the set of mutable triangles under a flip (faces adjacent to the flipped triangle lose a side)

ideas.what: Additivity of gradations along arcs subdivided under specialization, and the request for a notion of graded sub-polygon with commuting 'déploiements'.
ideas.modern_name: Weighted subdivision / compatibility of edge weights under refinement

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets out to axiomatize the local structure at each configuration of the specialization graph of pseudo-line systems. The intended axioms are cyclic polygon, antipody, gradations, and sub-polygon embeddings under specialization. He then asks (next page) whether these restriction maps are determined by the other structures. This 'local-to-global combinatorial presentation' of the arrangement space is not carried out in this form in the literature.
missed.quote: On trouve ... isomorphisme de Pol*(D) avec un sous-polygone de Pol*(D'), mais ce n'est pas ici un isomorphisme
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a hands-on precursor to describing the topology of spaces of pseudo-line arrangements (the oriented-matroid Grassmannian/MacPhersonian, extension spaces) by local link data. It is mainly of historical interest unless the axiom system were completed.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an exploratory, partly undefined attempt to formalize the local link structure of the flip/specialization graph. The concrete mathematical fact (new triangles arise from adjacent quadrilaterals) is standard. The historically interesting part is Grothendieck's antipody-and-gradation formalism, which is not developed enough here to count as a missed result.
transcription_corrections: 'les antispécialisations des types cas' should read 'les antipodiques des cas' (the next page uses 'son antipodique est un sommet de spécialisation'); likewise '(pointées, antispécialisées)' is probably '(pointées, antipodiques)'.
'NB La pseudo-situation d'une arête de Pol*(D) peut être nulle' should read 'NB La pondération d'une arête de Pol*(D) peut être nulle'.
'L'antidéformation de Pol*(D) est intrinsèque' should read 'L'antipodie de Pol*(D) est intrinsèque'.

'NB les pseudo-situations de Pol*(D)' / 'compatibilité avec les pseudo-situations' should read 'les pondérations' / 'compatibilité avec les pondérations'; the margin note says the weights are 'stables par antipodie'.
'arête libre de Γ(X)' is very likely 'Γ(Σ)'.
'il serait pratique d'adjoindre' is written over a struck-out phrase; the underlined 'il serait pratique' is the retained reading.
